sections.h2: Does Iowa's landlord tenant law cover a rental house you want to sell?
sections.html:
Usually, yes. The Iowa Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, Chapter 562A of the Iowa Code, covers ordinary rental houses, duplexes and apartments. It applies to agreements entered into, extended or renewed after January 1, 1979.

A short list of arrangements falls outside it: contract purchasers, employees housed as a condition of the job, hotel and motel stays, owners of condominiums and co-ops, farm rentals, and some nonprofit transitional housing. Mobile home communities fall under a separate chapter, 562B. If your tenant fits one of those exclusions, the rules below may not match your situation, so read the statute or talk to an Iowa attorney first.

Two definitions help with a sale. A "resident" is an occupant at least 18 years old. A "single family residence" has its own street access and shares no heat, hot water or essential facility with another unit. A rental house you own outright usually meets that description.

sections.h2: What happens to the lease when a landlord sells
sections.html:
A lease does not end because the owner sells. Chapter 562A gives a seller no way to cancel a fixed-term lease on closing day, so the buyer normally takes the property with the tenant and the lease in place.

Three parts of the statute come into play at closing:

  • Deposit transfer. Under 562A.12, the deposit, less lawful deductions, goes to the new owner, who must notify the tenant, or it is returned to the tenant. A new owner who tells the tenant in writing what the deposit amount is may rely on that figure if the tenant does not object within 20 days.
  • Disclosure duties. Under 562A.13, the duty to disclose the owner's and manager's names and addresses carries over to a successor owner.
  • Release from later liability. Under 562A.16, a seller who sells in good faith to a bona fide purchaser is relieved of liability for later events once the tenant receives written notice of the sale.

In practice, send the tenant a dated written notice with the buyer's name and the address for rent and repair requests.

sections.h2: Iowa notice periods and dollar limits
sections.html:
These are the main numbers a rental owner works with under Chapter 562A.

Landlord duty or limitIowa rule
Security deposit capTwo months' rent
Deposit return30 days after the tenancy ends and the tenant gives a mailing address
Rent increaseWritten notice at least 30 days before it takes effect, and not before the term or renewal ends
Landlord entry24 hours' notice at reasonable times, except emergencies
Late fee cap, rent up to $700$12 a day or $60 a month
Late fee cap, rent over $700$20 a day or $100 a month
Nonpayment of rentThree days after written notice to pay
Other material breachSeven days to cure after written notice
Month-to-month ending30 days before the periodic rental date
Week-to-week ending10 days

An Iowa landlord must return the deposit or send an itemized written statement within 30 days after the tenancy ends and the tenant provides a mailing address. A landlord who misses that deadline loses the right to withhold anything.

The other deposit rules are just as specific:

  • The deposit must sit in an insured institution and may not be mixed with the landlord's own money.
  • Interest earned in the first five years belongs to the landlord.
  • The landlord carries the burden of proving that a deduction was justified.
  • Bad-faith retention can bring punitive damages up to twice the monthly rent, plus actual damages.
  • If the tenant never supplies an address within one year, the deposit reverts to the landlord.

Before you list or sell a rental, find the deposit records and reconcile them. A buyer or title company will ask where the money is, and a gap here can slow a closing.

sections.h2: Can a tenant stop you from showing the rental?
sections.html:
A tenant may not unreasonably refuse access to purchasers, and a landlord may enter after giving at least 24 hours' notice at reasonable times. In an emergency, no notice is needed.

The same section limits landlords. Entering when the law does not allow it, entering at unreasonable times, or using repeated entry demands to harass a tenant lets the tenant seek an injunction or end the lease. Damages then are at least one month's rent, plus fees (562A.35). If you plan several showings, write down the dates and give each notice early.

A tenant who refuses lawful access can face an injunction or lease termination, along with damages and fees.

Iowa landlords must follow the housing codes that affect health and safety, keep the unit fit and habitable, and keep supplied facilities working. That covers plumbing, electrical systems, heating, running water and reasonable hot water, plus clean common areas and waste receptacles (562A.15).

If a landlord falls short, tenants have several routes under the act:

  • Written notice of a material breach, followed by termination if the problem is not fixed within seven days (562A.21).
  • Buying substitute service and deducting the cost, if the landlord cuts heat, water or other essentials on purpose or through neglect (562A.23).
  • Leaving and ending the lease within 14 days after fire or other casualty that substantially impairs use, or paying reduced rent if part of the unit is usable (562A.25).
  • Deducting repair costs, up to one month's rent, when defending a nonpayment claim, if the tenant gave seven days' notice before the rent was due (562A.27).

A buyer will ask about open repair complaints on a rental. Unresolved code issues also feed the retaliation risk described next.

Iowa bars a landlord from raising rent, cutting services or filing for possession because a tenant complained to a code agency, complained about a 562A.15 problem, or joined a tenants' union. A good-faith complaint made within the prior year creates a presumption of retaliation (562A.36).

A landlord also cannot remove a tenant by his or her own action. Utility shutoffs, changing locks and similar steps are barred except for abandonment, surrender or what the chapter allows (562A.33). A tenant who is locked out or cut off may recover possession or end the lease, and can seek actual damages, punitive damages up to twice the monthly rent, and attorney fees (562A.26).

Timing a sale to push out a tenant who recently complained is the kind of move this section targets. If you plan to sell and the tenant has complained in the past year, get advice before you send any notice.

sections.h2: How an Iowa eviction case moves through court
sections.html:
An eviction starts with a written notice, goes to a court filing under Chapter 648, and ends with removal by an officer only after a judgment. For unpaid rent, the usual first step is a three-day written notice to quit.

Once a case is filed, Iowa Code 648.5 sets the pace:

  • The court sets a hearing no later than eight days after filing, or up to 15 days if the plaintiff asks or agrees.
  • The tenant must be served at least three days before the hearing, by a signed acknowledgment from a resident aged 18 or older, personal service, or posting plus mailing after two failed attempts.
  • If judgment goes to the landlord, an execution for removal issues within three days, and removal happens in daytime only (648.20 and 648.22).
  • Thirty days of peaceable possession with the landlord's knowledge after the cause of action arose bars the proceeding (648.18).

Notices follow their own service rules: signed acknowledgment, personal service, or posting on the main entrance door plus regular and certified mail. Mailed notice is complete four days after deposit (562A.8 and 562A.29A).

sections.h2: Selling a tenant-occupied rental as is
sections.html:
Tenant rights add steps to a sale, but they do not block one. The tenant keeps the lease, the deposit follows the property, and written notice protects the seller from later claims.

Even a cash buyer inherits the tenancy if the house is occupied, so a clean file helps. Gather these items before you request an offer:

  • The signed lease and any renewals.
  • Deposit amount and where it is held.
  • Dates of repairs, code complaints and entry notices.
  • A draft written notice of the sale for the tenant.

With those papers in hand, the title company can confirm the deposit transfer and the buyer can see exactly what lease terms come with the house. If the tenant is month-to-month, remember that either side can end the tenancy on written notice at least 30 days before the periodic rental date. A fixed-term lease stays in place through closing.

faqs.q: Can an Iowa landlord end a lease just because the house is being sold?
faqs.a: No. Chapter 562A gives no special right to end a lease because of a sale, so a tenant with a fixed term generally stays until it ends. A month-to-month tenancy can be ended by either side with written notice at least 30 days before the periodic rental date.

faqs.q: How much notice must an Iowa landlord give before showing the house?
faqs.a: At least 24 hours, and the visit must happen at reasonable times. Emergencies are the exception. A tenant may not unreasonably refuse entry for showings to purchasers.

faqs.q: Who gets the security deposit when an Iowa rental is sold?
faqs.a: The deposit, less lawful deductions, goes to the new owner, who must tell the tenant, or it is returned to the tenant. The buyer then takes on the deposit duties. The seller should document the amount in writing.

faqs.q: How long does an Iowa landlord have to return a deposit?
faqs.a: Thirty days after the tenancy ends and the landlord receives the tenant's mailing address. The landlord must either return the money or send an itemized written statement of reasons for withholding.

faqs.q: Can I sell an Iowa rental house that has a tenant in it?
faqs.a: Yes. The tenant keeps the lease and the rights under it, and the buyer steps into the landlord role. Give the tenant written notice of the sale, transfer the deposit properly and keep records of repairs and notices.
